title: The sun visits his son
hookLine: the sun visits the son he grew apart from and is welcomed with black sesame; why Sankranti sweets come with sweet words
carry: sankranti mends bonds: sweet sesame, sweet words
last: MAKAR SANKRANTI: BEGIN IN THE LIGHT.

lines: A FATHER AND A SON, APART.
THE SUN AT HIS SON'S DOOR.
cards: Surya, the sun, has a son named Shani, the slow, serious planet people worry about. Their story isn't a happy one.
In many tellings, Surya kept his distance from the boy, Shani grew up hurt, and father and son hardly spoke. But the sun keeps moving, sign to sign, all year.
And Makara, the sign the sun enters at Sankranti, belongs in Hindu astrology to Shani. It's his house. So once a year the father arrives at his son's door.
And the son has to decide how to open it.

teach.b: As many families tell it, Shani's house had almost nothing in it. All he could offer was black sesame. He gave it to his father anyway, and Surya was moved, and blessed him, and father and son made peace.
It's a folk story, not from the old epics, but it's one of the reasons people give for why sesame is everywhere on this day.
In Maharashtra, people go visiting with little sweets of sesame and jaggery, the dark unrefined sugar, called til-gul.

You hand one to a neighbor, a cousin, a friend you've had words with, and say: til-gul ghya, god god bola. Take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. Sesame is small and sticks together; jaggery is sweet.
Here's the teaching. Hindus treat speech as part of dharma, the right way to live.

teach.h: SPEAK WHAT IS TRUE, AND SPEAK IT KINDLY.
teach.b: An old Sanskrit verse puts it plainly: speak what is true, and speak it kindly.

And Sankranti, the first day of the bright half, is a day for mending bonds and for dana, a gift given freely. People bathe at dawn, in a river if they can, and give sesame, grain, blankets or food to someone in need.
In Punjab, the night before is Lohri, with bonfires; in Assam, Bhogali Bihu, a feast.
And today: a sesame sweet is a small way to say what's hard to say out loud. Sorry. Let's start again.
If a father and a son who barely spoke could do it at a door, two friends can do it with a sweet.

how: On Makar Sankranti many Hindus bathe at dawn in a river, give food, grain or blankets to those in need, and share sweets of sesame and jaggery with the words 'take this, and speak sweetly'; the day is kept as Lohri, Bhogali Bihu and Pongal in different regions.

o: the sun's winter crossing, kept with sesame, sweet words and gifts
the night Lakshmi visits homes that keep a lamp lit
a spring feast marking the end of the wheat harvest

games.q: sesame and sweet words — tap the pairs.
p: the son the sun visits at Sankranti

s: the sesame sweet comes with words
til-gul ghya, god god bola: take this, and speak sweetly.
in the story, Shani welcomed his father with gold
he had only black sesame, and he offered it anyway.
giving is said to count especially on this day
sesame, blankets, grain, food: dana, a gift given freely.

games.q: it's Sankranti. you and a friend had a fight this week. you're holding a box of til-gul. what fits the day?
o: hand them a sweet and say: let's speak sweetly.
leave the box on their step and walk away.
games.why: the sweet goes hand to hand, with the old line: take this sesame and jaggery, and speak sweetly. Sankranti is for mending.

practice: Think of one person you've had sharp words with this year, small or big. Picture pressing one sesame sweet into their palm, no speech, just: take this, and let's speak sweetly.
Maybe their face softens, maybe it doesn't; that part isn't yours. If you pray, ask for kind speech this year, in your own words. Your part is the sweet and the words.

wordCard.voice: Makar Sankranti. The sun's crossing into Shani's sign, kept with sesame and sweet words, a dawn bath, and a gift given freely.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a gift given freely. Sankranti is one of the days when it's said to count most.

carryVoice: Your line: sankranti mends bonds: sweet sesame, sweet words. Tomorrow, a pot that's meant to boil over. See you then.

sources.ref: Folk telling of Surya visiting his son Shani at Makar Sankranti (black sesame); Makara as Shani's sign in jyotisha
Manusmriti 4.138 (speak the truth, speak what is pleasant)
Makar Sankranti observance: til-gul (Maharashtra), dawn bathing, dana; regional names Lohri, Bhogali (Magh) Bihu, Pongal
